questions.q: Identify the two supporting characters explicitly named or referenced in the poem "Blood" by Kamala Das.
questions.a: The two supporting characters are the great-grandmother and the speaker's brother. A wrong answer (e.g., listing the prince, the rats, or the snake-gods) reveals the student cannot distinguish between characters who actively participate in the poem's human drama and those who are merely part of the setting or backstory.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the great-grandmother says her feasts were "monotonous / For the only dish was always God".
questions.a: The great-grandmother means her life was devoted entirely to religious observance; spiritual practice was her sole sustenance, while worldly pleasures were mere "condiments" — minor additions. A wrong answer that interprets this literally (e.g., "she only ate one type of food") shows the student misses the metaphorical language and the characterization of the great-grandmother as deeply pious and detached from material luxury.

questions.q: The poem states: "She told us / That we had the oldest blood / My brother and she and I / The oldest blood in the world". Apply the concept of dramatic irony: what does the speaker understand about this claim *now* that she did not understand as a child?
questions.a: As a child, the speaker believed the great-grandmother's claim of aristocratic purity; as an adult, she recognizes it as a comforting myth that masks the reality of decay (the crumbling house) and her own failure to fulfill the promise to rebuild. A wrong answer that merely repeats the claim without the adult speaker's retrospective irony shows the student cannot track the shift in perspective across time.

questions.q: Analyze how the brother functions as a foil to the speaker. Use two specific textual details to support your answer.
questions.a: The brother is mentioned only as a passive companion ("My brother and I / And always playing on the sands") and never speaks or acts independently. He shares the childhood promise but disappears from the narrative, highlighting the speaker's solitary burden of memory and guilt. A wrong answer that invents actions for the brother or treats him as an equal protagonist shows the student cannot infer character function from minimal textual presence.

questions.q: Evaluate the great-grandmother's statement that the blood of "the always poor" and "the new-rich men" is "thick as gruel / And muddy as a ditch". Is this the poet's view or the character's view? Justify your judgment.
questions.a: This is the great-grandmother's feudal, classist worldview, not the poet's. The adult speaker later rejects this hierarchy by acknowledging her own "thin, clear, fine" blood remembers "gems and gold" but also by admitting she "let you down / Old house" and asking forgiveness — showing she no longer equates worth with lineage. A wrong answer that endorses the great-grandmother's snobbery as the poem's message reveals the student cannot separate character voice from authorial intent.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza from the brother's perspective, set years after the poem ends, that reveals his response to the house's destruction and the great-grandmother's death.
questions.a: A strong answer will reflect the brother's absence from the speaker's later life (e.g., living elsewhere, having forgotten the promise, or embodying the "new-rich" practicality the great-grandmother despised). A weak answer that merely repeats the speaker's guilt or describes the house again shows the student cannot imagine an independent consciousness for a marginal character.
